messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Vignette:
Elena Morales is a 78-year-old retired school librarian who still works part-time in a neighborhood library branch in an American city with a large Spanish-speaking community. She came to treatment after decades of keeping one part of her life tightly sealed off, a habit that had become harder to maintain as she grew older. Elena had come to the United States as a refugee when she was a young woman, after fleeing political violence in her home country in Latin America. When she speaks about that period, her account narrows and falters. She can give the outline—there was unrest, armed men, people disappearing, a hurried departure—but when she approaches the worst moment, language seems to fail her. She stops, presses a hand to her mouth, and says there are things she knows in her body that she “cannot really say.”

What emerges in fragments is that during her flight she was caught in a chaotic, terrifying scene marked by smoke, sweat, and the sharp, acrid smell of fuel and burning materials. The sensory quality of that moment has remained far more accessible to her than a coherent narrative. Even now, when she begins to think about what happened, she sometimes smells it again as if it were present around her, and the smell alone is enough to make her go still and distant. She does not describe this as remembering in an ordinary way. It is more like being pulled toward something she dreads and cannot fully represent in words. Alongside that comes a surge of guilt that feels immediate and personal, as if she is once again being confronted with what she believes she failed to do. Over the years she has gone over and over why it happened to her, searching for an explanation that never settles anything. Just as often, the question turns inward and hardens into self-blame. She has repeatedly returned to the thought that she must have done something wrong, missed something, or survived at some cost she still does not know how to justify.

In the years after arriving in the United States, Elena built a life defined by steadiness and order. She married, raised a family, and found work among shelves, catalog cards, and routines that were soothing in their predictability. Being busy became one of the central ways she managed herself. If she kept moving—reshelving books, helping patrons, checking returns, straightening displays, cooking, folding laundry, keeping appointments—there was less room for the old questions to come forward. Her husband learned that she preferred not to linger over the past. To others, she appeared disciplined and devoted; inside, she was often working hard to stay ahead of her own mind.

Even in apparently safe years, Elena remained intensely watchful. At the library she notices who comes through the door, where people stand, what bags they are carrying, how loud voices become. If there is commotion near the entrance, her attention fixes there immediately and she struggles to return to whatever she was doing. She has become aware that her concentration is not what she wants it to be. While checking out a stack of books for a patron, she can suddenly realize she has read the same title twice without taking it in, because part of her mind is scanning the room. The library, despite its quiet, is not uniformly comfortable to her; she feels safest only in a small number of places she knows intimately, especially her own home, her workstation behind the circulation desk, and a particular reading room with a single door and a clear view of who enters. Outside those limited places, she feels exposed in a way she cannot easily explain to her family.

Over months and years, these patterns narrowed her life. She declined outings that took her far from familiar settings. She left errands to her husband when stores felt too crowded or unfamiliar. At work she kept to tasks that allowed her to remain in the parts of the building she trusted, and she felt ashamed that after so many years in the country she still organized herself this way. The shame fused easily with the guilt she already carried. More recently, as retirement reduced the amount of busyness available to her, there were longer stretches in which the old sensory impressions returned. The smell would come first, then the guilt, then the relentless circling over why it had happened and what she should have done differently.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but the recognition that her world had grown too small. After freezing at work when a patron’s gasoline can, left briefly near the entrance for a community event, sent a smell through the lobby, she went home shaken and embarrassed. She told her husband, with difficulty, that she was tired of living as if safety existed only in a few corners. She is frightened that if she speaks more plainly about the past, the guilt will become unbearable, but she is also hoping, cautiously, that she might find a way to remember without being overtaken by what her body still seems to know better than words.
